content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
Describe examples of inherited disorders including cystic fibrosis and polydactyly
Explain the inheritance patterns of dominant and recessive disorders
Use genetic diagrams to predict the probability of inheriting disorders
Discuss the implications of genetic screening and testing

(or genetic disorder) is a condition caused by a faulty allele that can be passed from parents to children. Some disorders are caused by dominant alleles, while others are caused by recessive alleles. Understanding inheritance patterns helps families understand their risk and make informed decisions.
One copy of faulty allele causes disorder
Two copies of faulty allele needed
On X chromosome; mainly affects males
is a genetic disorder affecting the lungs, digestive system, and other organs.
Mutation in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7
Thick, sticky mucus in lungs → breathing difficulties, infections
Mucus blocks pancreatic ducts → digestive problems
The CFTR protein is a chloride ion channel:
Normal CFTR allows chloride ions to move out of cells
Water follows by osmosis, keeping mucus thin
1 in 2 (50%) chance of being a carrier
1 in 4 (25%) chance of being normal (not carrier)
About 1 in 25 people in UK are carriers
About 1 in 2,500 babies born with CF
is having extra fingers or toes.
Only ONE copy of the faulty allele is needed
Affected individuals usually have an affected parent
50% risk if one parent is heterozygous affected
is a blood disorder where red blood cells become sickle (crescent) shaped.
Carriers (Hb^A Hb^S) have some protection against malaria:
The sickle cell allele is more common in areas with malaria
is a neurodegenerative disorder causing progressive brain damage.
Symptoms usually appear in middle age (30-50 years)
One copy of the faulty allele causes the disease
50% chance of inheriting if one parent is affected
Symptoms appear after reproductive age (can be passed on before diagnosis)
Genetic testing can identify carriers before symptoms appear
Raises ethical questions about testing and family planning

Risk of miscarriage with invasive tests

Genetic disorders only affect one sex
Autosomal disorders affect males and females equally (sex-linked disorders differ)
Carriers of recessive disorders are usually completely healthy
If parents are healthy, their children can't have a genetic disorder

Inherited disorders are caused by faulty alleles passed from parents to children
Recessive disorders (e.g., cystic fibrosis) require two copies of the faulty allele
Dominant disorders (e.g., polydactyly) only require one copy
Carriers of recessive disorders are unaffected but can pass on the allele
Genetic testing can identify carriers and affected individuals
Testing raises ethical considerations about privacy, discrimination, and reproductive choices
